passages.t: ‘Shall we continue in sin?’ Baptized into his death
passages.happening:
Paul raises the obvious objection to everything he has said about grace. “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?” (verse 1).

“Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?” (verse 2).

Then he reminds them what their baptism meant. “Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?” (verse 3).

“We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The objection was real. Paul had already been slandered for teaching that people should do evil so that good may come (3:8). And 5:20 had just said that where sin increased, grace increased all the more. Someone could twist that into: then sin more, and get more grace.

Paul's answer is not a rule but a fact about who believers are. They have ‘died to sin’. A dead man does not go back to his old life.

He points to something every believer in Rome had been through: baptism. In the early church baptism was how a person entered the community of believers. It was in water, and often, it seems, by going right under the water. The New Testament does not describe exactly how it was done. Many readers think Paul has that picture in mind: going down into the water like a burial, coming up like a rising.

‘Baptized into Christ Jesus’ means joined to him, so that what happened to him counts for them. His death becomes theirs. His rising becomes the start of their new life.

‘Newness of life’ does not mean a slightly better life. It means a life of a new kind, lived from the other side of death.
passages.ot:
Israel's own story had a passage through water from slavery to freedom. At the Red Sea “the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left” (Exodus 14:29). Paul uses that crossing as a picture of baptism in another letter (1 Corinthians 10:1-2).

The prophets promised a cleansing and a new heart: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25), and “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.hard:
What does baptism do? Here every church agrees on a great deal. Baptism, Paul says, joins a believer to Christ's death and resurrection. It is commanded by Christ, it marks entry into his people, and it calls the baptized to a new life. Paul says the same elsewhere: “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

Churches differ on how baptism and faith relate, on whether baptism itself conveys forgiveness and new birth, on baptizing infants, and on the way water is used. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches see baptism as God's work that truly gives what it signifies. Reformed churches see it as a sign and seal of God's promise. Baptists and many evangelicals see it as the believer's public sign of faith already given. The note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out these readings in their holders' own words. These notes do not choose. All agree that baptism points to Christ, and that the baptized are called to walk in newness of life.
passages.asks: ‘How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?’ Ask what sin you treat as harmless because you know you will be forgiven. Then remember your baptism, or think about it if you have not been baptized. Ask what it says about who you are now, and whose life you are now living.

passages.t: Dead to sin, alive to God
passages.happening:
If we have been united with Christ in his death, we will certainly be united with him in his resurrection (verse 5). “We know that our old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer be slaves to sin” (verse 6). Anyone who has died has been freed from sin (verse 7).

If we died with Christ, we believe we will also live with him (verse 8). Christ, raised from the dead, cannot die again; death has no more power over him (verse 9). He died to sin once for all, and the life he lives, he lives to God (verse 10).

“So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (verse 11).

So do not let sin reign in your mortal body (verse 12). Do not offer the parts of your body to sin “as instruments of wickedness”, but offer yourselves to God, as people brought from death to life, and your bodies to him “as instruments of righteousness” (verse 13).

“For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
‘Our old self’ means the person you were before you belonged to Christ, the self that lived under the rule of sin. Paul says it was ‘crucified with Him’. That happened, in God's eyes, when Christ died.

‘Count yourselves dead to sin’. The word ‘count’ is the same bookkeeping word Paul used of Abraham being credited with righteousness. Believers are to reckon as true what God says is true about them, and then live by it.

‘Instruments’ is the Greek hoplon, which usually meant weapons, a soldier's arms. Paul pictures a war. Each part of the body, eyes, hands, tongue, feet, is a weapon that can be handed to one side or the other.

‘Do not let sin reign’ shows that sin still pushes. Paul does not say believers never feel its pull. He says it is no longer the king, and they must not hand it the crown.

‘Not under law, but under grace’ is the reason sin will not be master. The law could name sin but not break its power. Grace both forgives and gives a new life.
passages.ot:
The Psalms speak of God breaking a servant's bonds: “Truly, O LORD, I am Your servant; I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant; You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 116:16).

The choice between two masters is as old as Joshua: “choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve” (Joshua 24:15).

Moses set the same choice before Israel: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19).
passages.hard: If believers have died to sin, why do Christians still sin? Paul's own commands show that sin still tugs, or he would not need to say ‘do not let sin reign’. Christians explain this in more than one way. Most say Paul describes a change of master and power, not the end of temptation: sin has been thrown off the throne, but still tries to give orders. Reformed and Lutheran churches stress that sin remains in believers until death, though its rule is broken. The Wesleyan tradition teaches that by grace a believer may come to love God so fully that deliberate sin no longer rules, while still being open to mistakes and weakness. All agree that the answer to ongoing sin is not less grace but a deeper grasp of it.
passages.asks: Paul tells believers to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. Ask what you believe about yourself: that you are still a slave who cannot change, or someone set free. Then take one part of your body, your tongue, your eyes, your hands, and ask whose side it fought on today.

passages.t: Slaves of righteousness, and the gift of God
passages.happening:
“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!” (verse 15).

Whoever you obey, Paul says, you are that one's slave: either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness (verse 16). But thanks be to God that, though you were once slaves to sin, you wholeheartedly obeyed the teaching you were given (verse 17). “You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness” (verse 18).

“I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh” (verse 19). Just as you once offered your body to impurity and ever-growing wickedness, now offer it to righteousness, leading to holiness (verse 19).

When you were slaves to sin, you were free from righteousness (verse 20). What did you gain from the things you are now ashamed of? They end in death (verse 21). But now, set free from sin and made slaves to God, you gain holiness, and the end is eternal life (verse 22).

“For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, and in Rome itself a large part of the people were slaves or former slaves. Some of the believers who first heard this letter were probably slaves. They knew what it meant to belong to a master, to obey, to be bought, and sometimes to be set free. A freed slave often still owed duties to his former master.

So Paul's picture would have hit hard. Everyone serves someone. The only question is which master. Sin is a master who pays in death. God is a master who sets free.

Then Paul does something unusual: he apologises for the picture. ‘I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh.’ Many readers take him to mean that the picture is too crude for life with God, who is a Father and not an owner, but that he uses it because his hearers will grasp it: belonging to God is total.

‘Wages’ (Greek opsōnion) was used of a soldier's pay. Sin pays its wages faithfully, and the wage is death. God does not pay wages at all. He gives a gift, the same word family as grace.

Paul's use of the picture is not approval of slavery. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces that question honestly.
passages.ot:
Israel's story begins with God freeing slaves: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Because of that, the law said, “Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves” (Leviticus 25:42). To belong to God was to belong to no other master.

The link between sin and death goes back to Eden: “in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die” (Genesis 2:17). Ezekiel says, “The soul who sins is the one who will die” (Ezekiel 18:4).
passages.hard:
Is Paul approving of slavery when he uses it as a picture? No. He borrows a picture his hearers knew, and he apologises for it as he does so (verse 19). Elsewhere he tells a master to receive his runaway slave “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). The Bible's own law made kidnapping a person to sell him a crime worthy of death (Exodus 21:16). Yet Christians for centuries used other verses to defend slavery, and that was a grievous wrong. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces the whole question without softening it.

‘The wages of sin is death’ is also often quoted on its own. In Romans it is half a sentence. The other half is the point: ‘the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord’.
passages.asks: Paul says everyone serves some master. Ask honestly what has been giving you orders: a habit, a fear, money, other people's approval. What wages has it paid you? Then read verse 23 to the end. Eternal life is not a wage you earn but a gift you receive. Ask whether you have received it.
